sentences.text: The animal is known as Infernogallus, a genus containing only one species, Infernogallus jamesi.
This small dinosaur had an estimated body mass of approximately 12 kg, with the holotype specimen weighing between 9 and 15 kg.

Fossil material includes a partial articulated skull and skeleton, featuring a large circular eye hole occupying nearly 40% of the skull's length and an extremely small infratemporal fenestra measuring only 25% of the orbit's diameter.
Fossils of this animal have been found in the United States, specifically within the Hell Creek Formation in Montana, North Dakota, and South Dakota.
Currently, five specimens of Infernogallus are known to science.
Histological analysis of the bones revealed growth marks indicating skeletal maturity, suggesting the animal was at least 6, likely 7, years old when it died.
It likely had a specialized herbivorous diet consisting largely of fleshy angiosperm fruits, processed using anteroposterior mandible movement and ridges on opposing jaw elements.
Infernogallus is classified as a caenagnathid theropod dinosaur belonging to the family Caenagnathidae and is an oviraptorosaurian theropod.
This animal lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age, a time when caenagnathids originated soon after the appearance of fleshy angiosperm fruits known as drupes.
While the jaw muscle arrangement may represent an adaptation for fruit eating, it is debated whether this specific trait was indeed for that purpose.

Researchers cautioned against formally establishing subclades like 'elmisaurins' and 'caenagnathins' due to instability and inconsistency in interrelationships, though they noted certain groupings persisted.
It remains unclear what role caenagnathids like Infernogallus played in the Late Cretaceous proliferation of fruit.
